title: The USO tour band and the trip to Japan
summary: Oscar Pettiford organizes a six-piece USO band with J.J. Johnson, Skeeter Best and Rudy Williams; they play radar camps and travel to Japan then Korea.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well, now we're getting up towards the Fifties.
Yeah, it's '49 we're at now.
Right.
In the Fifties, I went to Korea and so forth.

Well, that was an interesting trip, which the Institute is very interested in. Of course, you and I have talked about this story before, but I think we should go into it in some detail. It was a USO tour.

Yeah. Well, Oscar had met this doctor from Orange, New Jersey or somewhere, and they had talked him into getting a six-piece group together so that we could play the USO camps -- which he did. We all got together. First we had Budd Johnson on tenor, and then we switched over and got Rudy Williams. It was a good band.
J.J.
Yeah, with J.J. it was something else, man. He added a lot to the band. Because he's one guy who knows his instrument. He knows how to play the trumpet, too.
And you had Charlie Rice and Skeeter Best...

Charlie, yeah. Well, Skeeter was a good guitarist. I don't know why now he ain't too playing too good. He's getting over or something. They say he ain't playing right. I don't know. I haven't heard him lately.
Now, you did the USO bases at Okinawa and the Philippines...

First we did all the radar camps here in America. We did all the way out to the State of Washington and back, and all the way through northern New York, and just doing these dates here. Then they decided to send us to Korea, and they did -- they sent us over there. So we went to Japan, and we stayed there for about week, getting I guess the necessary shots you need to go to Korea. And then we we went to Korea and we played...
Did you play in Japan at all?
Well, yeah, but they were only where the American soldiers were. We didn't play for any...
You didn't play for the population.
No, not for the population we didn't play. We just played for the U.S. people until we got to Korea -- then we played for the gooks...and the people in the Army and Navy.
Had the Koreans never heard Jazz before?
Well, if they had, they didn't act like it.
What was their reaction?
They liked it all right, but they didn't know exactly what it was. Because we were playing from soup to nuts. Like, we started out with "When Jazz first started," you know...
It was like a little history of Jazz.

A history of Jazz, right. But I mean, they liked it all right. But you know, anywhere you go, they still like Dixieland. So we played Dixieland everywhere. They went, "Oh yeah, yeah, that's American music, all right." Ha-ha! I said, "That's just some American music. I couldn't come right out and lay it out... So that's the way it went.
